bases.narrative: My mother can't live on her own any more. My brother Daniel and I are making this decision together; Mom has told us she will go along with whatever the two of us agree. Her doctor says she can stay safely in her own house with a daytime aide, or move into Maple Court, an assisted-living home. Maple Court charges $6,200 a month, and her long-term-care policy pays $1,500 a month toward a facility but nothing toward home care. An aide would work 30 hours a week at $40 an hour, and we count a month as 52/12 weeks. Maple Court is six minutes from my apartment; Mom's house is 35 minutes away. Our rule: we will move Mom into Maple Court if and only if Maple Court's monthly rate minus what her policy pays is lower than the aide's monthly cost; otherwise we will hire the aide. Nothing else is part of this decision for Daniel and me.
bases.question: Should we move Mom into Maple Court or hire a daytime aide?

options.text: Hire a daytime aide so Mom stays in her house

bases.narrative: Our furnace is 19 years old and needs a $2,000 repair to get through another winter. The alternative is replacing it with a heat pump, quoted at $11,900 installed; the state rebate takes $3,000 off that. The installer says the heat pump would cut our heating bill by about $60 a month, and it would take the house off gas completely. My wife Ana and I are deciding this together. We'll install the heat pump if and only if its installed price minus the state rebate comes to less than $8,000 more than the furnace repair; otherwise we'll repair the furnace. Nothing else is part of this decision for us.
bases.question: Should we install the heat pump or repair the furnace?

options.text: Replace the furnace with a heat pump

Nothing else is part of this decision for us.

bases.narrative: Our daughter Priya starts kindergarten in the fall. She got a seat at Ridgeview Magnet; otherwise she goes to Lincoln, our neighbourhood school, which is a short walk away. The district route sheet puts the Ridgeview bus ride at 34 minutes, plus a 10-minute walk to the stop. Ridgeview's after-care ends at 4:30; Lincoln's runs to 6:00. Nine of her preschool friends are going to Lincoln and two to Ridgeview. My wife Dana and I decide this between us. We'll send her to Ridgeview if and only if the bus ride plus the walk to the stop adds up to less than 50 minutes; otherwise she goes to Lincoln. Everything else about the two schools is close enough that it doesn't enter into it for us.

bases.narrative: I'm deciding whether to put solar panels on my house. The installer quoted $20,000, the federal tax credit covers 30% of that, and the installer estimates the panels would save me $1,300 a year on electricity. They would cut my grid use by about 60%. I expect to stay in this house another 12 years. My partner has said this one is my call alone. I'll install solar if and only if the price after the tax credit, divided by the yearly savings, comes to fewer years than I expect to stay; otherwise I'll skip it. Nothing else is part of this decision for me.
bases.question: Should I install the solar panels or skip solar?

bases.narrative: I'm choosing how to get to work for the next two years. The e-bike I want costs $2,400, upkeep runs about $250 a year, and the city gives a $400 rebate on e-bikes. I'll buy the e-bike if and only if its price plus two years of upkeep, minus the city rebate, is less than two years of transit passes; otherwise I'll buy the pass. Nothing else is part of this decision for me.
